haiku-low.q1: MySQL commits first, and the same transaction adds a pending row. The request then tries copying to Postgres. If that fails, the request still succeeds and the sweeper retries.
haiku-low.q2: Only when no tombstone exists for the id and the existing row's version is lower than the incoming one, under the id's named lock.
haiku-low.q3: Every instance must show dual in app_flag_value for users.write_mode. Instances can disagree for up to 30 seconds after a flag change.
haiku-low.q4: It reads 2,000 rows per batch in primary-key order, checks replica lag before each batch, pauses above 5 seconds, and stops after about 50 seconds per run.
haiku-low.q5: Reads need a clean comparer pass (zero mismatches in one full pass) and a stepped flag rollout with error checks. The source of truth moves after 3 days at 100% reads, once a person sets the flag.
haiku-low.q6: A pending row in the source-of-truth database's pending table records that the other database is behind. The sweeper retries it each minute until the copy succeeds.
haiku-low.q7: A tombstone blocks any later copy of that id. Copies and deletes hold the same named lock and check tombstones, and the comparer removes leftover rows with tombstoned ids.
haiku-low.q8: Progress (last completed id) is saved in backfill_progress in MySQL, only after its batch is copied. A run resumes after that id, and it stops once backfill reaches the highest id.
haiku-low.q9: The comparer scans both tables in primary-key order and counts mismatches after rereading the source row. Mismatches are passed to the sweeper, which repairs them.
haiku-low.q10: Writes freeze to frozen, and every instance must show it before the switch, after a 10-second wait for in-flight writes. If pending rows do not drain in 15 seconds, set dual and retry later. The document does not say more.
haiku-low.q11: Postgres assigns ids in pg_primary from its sequence, set to the highest id in either database plus 1. The document does not state how collisions are avoided after a rollback, beyond MySQL's counter moving past explicit ids.
haiku-low.q12: Each write is copied back to MySQL for 14 days, and the comparer keeps running. Rollback sets frozen, drains Postgres pending rows into MySQL, then sets dual. It ends at step 10, pg_only.

sonnet.q1: The write commits to MySQL first (and adds the user id to MySQL's pending table in the same transaction), then the request tries to copy the row to Postgres. If the Postgres copy fails, the request still succeeds; the caller sees success and the pending row waits for the sweeper.
sonnet.q2: Only if the incoming row has a higher version than the existing Postgres row (existing has a lower version), and no tombstone exists for the id. Otherwise do nothing. It's done under the id's named lock in one transaction.
sonnet.q3: Every instance must report `dual` in `app_flag_value{flag="users.write_mode"}`; the scheduled worker refuses to start until then. Instances can disagree for up to 30 seconds (flag refresh interval).
sonnet.q4: It reads from the MySQL replica (not the primary) in primary-key order, 2,000 rows per batch. Before each batch it checks replica lag; if lag is above 5 seconds it stops and retries next minute (reporting jobs share the replica). Each run stops after about 50 seconds.
sonnet.q5: Reads: a clean comparer pass (a full pass with zero mismatches), then stepping the flag 1, 10, 50, 100 with error checks before each step. Source of truth: reads held at 100% on Postgres for 3 days, then a person sets the flag; also the freeze sequence must succeed (all instances show `frozen`, 10 second wait, MySQL pending table drained within 15 seconds, sequence set).
sonnet.q6: A pending-table row for the user id, written in the same transaction as the MySQL commit and so kept in MySQL (the source of truth). It survives a Postgres outage or app death. The sweeper (runs every minute, up to 500 oldest rows) reads the current row from MySQL and copies it to Postgres with the copy rule, removing the pending row only after success; failures are retried every minute.
sonnet.q7: Erasure writes a tombstone (and deletes the row, adds a pending row) in one transaction on the source of truth. Copies and deletes hold the same per-id named lock and the copy rule does nothing if a tombstone exists, so an in-flight copy cannot re-create the user. The comparer also finds and removes any row whose id has a tombstone.
sonnet.q8: Progress (last completed id) is stored in `backfill_progress` in MySQL, saved only after its batch has been copied. After a crash it resumes after the last saved id; the in-flight batch is copied again, which is harmless due to the version rule. It stops when it reaches the highest id (after which the comparer starts), and each run also stops after about 50 seconds or on lag above 5 seconds / Postgres unreachable.
sonnet.q9: The comparer scans both tables in primary-key order (2,000 rows per batch, same lag pause). It counts a mismatch when a row is missing in Postgres, version or fields differ, or a tombstoned id exists in Postgres, after rereading the row from the source of truth. Mismatches are passed to the sweeper, which repairs them with the copy rule (tombstoned rows are removed). Passes repeat until one finds zero mismatches.
sonnet.q10: Via a freeze: set `frozen` (all writes return retryable 503), wait until every instance shows `frozen` in the metric (up to 30 seconds), wait 10 seconds for in-flight writes, drain MySQL pending rows, set the Postgres sequence, then set `pg_primary`. No instance writes to the old source of truth, so no write is split. If pending doesn't drain within 15 seconds, set `dual` again and retry later. After step 5, an instance still on `frozen` returns 503 until it picks up the new value. Worst case is 85 seconds, within the 90-second limit.
sonnet.q11: The Postgres sequence assigns ids in `pg_primary`. At the switch it is set to the highest id in either database plus 1. Collisions are avoided because copies into MySQL keep explicit ids and InnoDB moves its AUTO_INCREMENT counter past any larger explicit id. After a rollback to `dual`, MySQL's counter stays ahead because of that. NOT STATED whether the doc explicitly addresses Postgres-sequence-created ids beyond this.
sonnet.q12: In `pg_primary`, each write commits to Postgres and is copied to MySQL, with failed copies left as pending rows in Postgres for the sweeper; the comparer keeps running. Rollback: set `frozen`, wait as in step 8, drain the Postgres pending rows into MySQL, then set `dual` (same 90-second limit). The option ends when `pg_only` is set in step 10, no sooner than 14 days after step 8, with the comparer clean and pending empty; it fully ends at the step 11 drop of the MySQL table.
